name: THC Encyclopedia Worked Example Visual Briefs
purpose: Production-ready visual briefs tied to high-value worked examples. Visuals must teach the reasoning, evidence, and verification method rather than decorate the page.

artDirection.style: academic studio-quality cultivation education; neutral/cream background; natural plant color; crisp scientific diagrams; restrained green/gold accents; no yellow cast; no decorative clutter
artDirection.textPolicy: Use concise labels, legends, and short callouts. Do not bake paragraph text into artwork.
artDirection.scientificPolicy: Visual must separate observation, measurement, interpretation, and verification. No unsupported universal thresholds or causal claims.
artDirection.accessibilityPolicy: Do not rely on color alone. Every state, comparison, or warning must also use labels, shapes, patterns, or position cues.
artDirection.copyrightPolicy: Create original artwork; sources constrain concepts and terminology only.
artDirection.publicationPolicy: Artwork remains artwork-needed until scientific QA, visual QA, label/spelling QA, accessibility QA, mobile crop QA, and placement QA all pass.

briefs.exampleTitle: Root decline after repeated wet irrigation
briefs.primaryMessage: Brown roots are evidence of root decline, not proof of one pathogen; diagnosis requires crop pattern, root-zone measurements, and organism evidence.
layout: Root-zone evidence panel: moisture, drainage, EC, temperature, irrigation history
Differential branch: abiotic predisposition / pathogen / mixed cause
Verification strip: intervention → repeat root/shoot observations → recheck measurements
forbiddenClaims: Do not label brown roots as a specific pathogen diagnosis
Do not imply wet media proves disease
Do not prescribe a universal irrigation frequency
briefs.altText: Diagnostic decision diagram showing brown-root decline, root-zone measurements, pathogen evidence, competing abiotic causes, and a verification loop.
briefs.caption: Root decline is interpreted from plant pattern, root-zone conditions, organism evidence, and follow-up—not from root color alone.

briefs.exampleTitle: VPD reading looks acceptable, leaves still show excessive demand
briefs.primaryMessage: A room VPD value does not prove every leaf experiences the same vapor-pressure conditions.
layout: Controller sensor vs canopy sensor positions
Context panel: light, airflow, root-zone water
forbiddenClaims: Do not show one VPD band as universally optimal
Do not equate controller value with leaf condition
Do not imply VPD alone diagnoses stress
briefs.altText: Environmental measurement diagram comparing controller VPD with canopy and leaf conditions, including sensor placement, leaf temperature, light, airflow, and root-zone context.
briefs.caption: VPD is a derived metric whose interpretation depends on where and how temperature and humidity are measured and on actual leaf conditions.

briefs.exampleTitle: A dryback percentage is copied from another facility
briefs.primaryMessage: Dryback only has meaning when the measured quantity, reference point, method, sensor location, and time interval are defined.
layout: Four measurement methods: VWC / sensor output / container mass / substrate potential
Interpretation panel with EC and plant response
forbiddenClaims: Do not present one dryback percentage as universal
Do not imply all sensor percentages are equivalent
Do not imply more dryback is always better
briefs.altText: Dryback measurement workflow showing different measurement bases, a post-irrigation reference, time-series change, sensor position, root-zone EC, and plant response.
briefs.caption: Dryback is a defined change over time, not a universal percentage that transfers unchanged between substrates, sensors, containers, and crops.

briefs.exampleTitle: High center PPFD, weak edge growth
briefs.primaryMessage: One center PPFD reading cannot describe canopy uniformity; use a repeatable spatial grid and preserve raw measurements.
layout: Center hotspot and edge low zones
forbiddenClaims: Do not use one center reading to characterize the whole canopy
Do not hide hotspots behind averages
Do not imply one uniformity target fits every room
briefs.altText: Top-down PPFD grid showing center hotspots, edge low-light zones, fixture geometry, raw readings, and before-after mapping.
briefs.caption: Spatial light mapping shows whether averages hide crop-relevant hotspots or low-light zones.

briefs.exampleTitle: Yellowing appears after a bloom-booster increase
briefs.primaryMessage: A deficiency-like symptom should be tested against root-zone chemistry, irrigation, roots, environment, and recent input changes before adding more nutrient.
forbiddenClaims: Do not equate yellowing with phosphorus deficiency
Do not recommend a fertilizer rate
Do not make runoff EC a stand-alone diagnosis
briefs.altText: Differential-diagnosis board connecting yellowing symptoms with root condition, pH, EC, irrigation, recent nutrient changes, competing explanations, and verification.
briefs.caption: Deficiency-like symptoms require root-zone and management evidence before a nutrient correction is justified.

briefs.exampleTitle: Clone matches genotype but performs differently
briefs.primaryMessage: Clones normally preserve inherited genotype while health, physiological state, propagation history, and environment can still change phenotype and performance.
layout: Parallel state variables: roots, pathogen status, reserves, environment
Decision panel: identity question vs performance question
forbiddenClaims: Do not imply clones are phenotypically identical
Do not imply poor performance proves mutation
Do not use genetic testing as a substitute for crop diagnosis
briefs.altText: Clone lineage diagram showing shared inherited genotype alongside differences in root quality, health, propagation history, environment, and phenotype.
briefs.caption: Clonal propagation preserves inherited genotype but not identical physiological state, health, or performance across conditions.

briefs.exampleTitle: One photo is labeled a nutrient deficiency
briefs.primaryMessage: Pattern, history, measurements, competing hypotheses, and verification should precede a product or diagnosis.
forbiddenClaims: Do not diagnose from one leaf photo
Do not treat the most common cause as automatically correct
Do not imply improvement after stacked changes proves the diagnosis
briefs.altText: Plant diagnostic workflow moving from a leaf observation to whole-crop pattern, root-zone and environmental evidence, ranked hypotheses, and controlled verification.
briefs.caption: A strong plant diagnosis explains the crop pattern, survives competing explanations, and is verified after a bounded correction.

briefs.exampleTitle: Dense flower rot is assumed to be Botrytis
briefs.primaryMessage: Flower rot should be described and sampled before assigning Botrytis or another pathogen identity.
layout: Microclimate context: condensation / dense canopy / airflow
forbiddenClaims: Do not label all gray/brown flower rot as Botrytis
Do not imply high RH proves infection
Do not treat a photo as pathogen confirmation
briefs.altText: Disease differential diagram showing flower-rot symptoms, pathogen signs, canopy microclimate, diagnostic sampling, and confidence-based identification.
briefs.caption: Botrytis diagnosis is strongest when signs, disease pattern, environment, and diagnostic evidence agree.

briefs.exampleTitle: Recurring pest problem despite calendar sprays
briefs.primaryMessage: Recurring pest pressure should trigger a prevention-and-monitoring review, not automatic escalation of calendar sprays.
layout: IPM loop: prevent → scout → identify → decide → act → verify
forbiddenClaims: Do not prescribe pesticide frequency
Do not imply IPM is pesticide rotation
Do not show one count reduction as proof of control
briefs.altText: Integrated pest management loop linking prevention, scouting, identification, decision thresholds, interventions, compatibility, and repeated verification.
briefs.caption: IPM is a recurring evidence-and-prevention system, not a calendar spray schedule.

briefs.exampleTitle: Drying room setpoint is stable but batches dry unevenly
briefs.primaryMessage: Stable room setpoints do not guarantee uniform product drying across racks and load geometry.
forbiddenClaims: Do not imply stable room RH guarantees uniform drying
Do not prescribe one universal setpoint
Do not hide position-dependent results in one average
briefs.altText: Drying-room map showing rack positions, airflow paths, load density, spatial measurements, and different drying curves across zones.
briefs.caption: Drying uniformity must be checked across the actual load because room averages can hide position effects.

briefs.exampleTitle: Small F2 population misses a rare trait combination
briefs.primaryMessage: Recovery of a desired F2 combination depends on trait architecture, probability, linkage, and population size.
forbiddenClaims: Do not imply simple Mendelian ratios apply to every trait
Do not imply absence in a small population proves impossibility
Do not show selected winners without the full population context
briefs.altText: F2 breeding diagram linking segregation and recombination with population size, recovery probability, observed classes, and model assumptions.
briefs.caption: Population size determines how well an F2 can sample rare favorable combinations under the stated genetic model.

briefs.exampleTitle: One phenotype wins in one room
briefs.primaryMessage: A strong phenotype in one location must be separated from room, position, season, and management effects before being called genetically superior.
forbiddenClaims: Do not equate one-room superiority with genetic superiority
Do not count subsamples as independent biological replicates
Do not hide failed or nonselected plants
briefs.altText: Breeding trial comparison showing a confounded single-room result versus replicated blocked or randomized testing with checks and environmental retesting.
briefs.caption: Replication and environmental control help separate genetic signal from room and position effects.

briefs.exampleTitle: New meter shows more decimal places
briefs.primaryMessage: Resolution, accuracy, precision, bias, and uncertainty are different measurement properties.
layout: Two meter displays with different decimals
forbiddenClaims: Do not imply more decimal places means more accuracy
Do not imply calibration removes all uncertainty
Do not equate close repeat readings with truth
briefs.altText: Measurement-quality diagram comparing display resolution, reference accuracy, repeatability, bias, uncertainty, and supported reported digits.
briefs.caption: Extra decimal places describe resolution, not whether the measurement is accurate or fit for the decision.

briefs.exampleTitle: One sensor is used to represent an entire room
briefs.primaryMessage: Representative sampling requires spatial and temporal coverage tied to the decision, not many readings from one convenient sensor.
layout: Room map with one central sensor
forbiddenClaims: Do not imply a central sensor is always representative
Do not treat repeated readings from one point as independent spatial samples
Do not use averages to erase extremes
briefs.altText: Sampling-plan diagram comparing one central sensor with a representative spatial grid and time-based measurements across room gradients.
briefs.caption: A sampling plan should represent the population and decision, not just produce many readings from one location.

briefs.exampleTitle: Testing two irrigation strategies without pseudoreplication
briefs.primaryMessage: Treatment replication depends on independently assigned experimental units; many plants inside one treated room are not many treatment replicates.
layout: Room A vs Room B confounded design
forbiddenClaims: Do not count plants within one treatment room as independent room-level replicates
Do not imply two rooms alone prove causation
Do not imply more subsamples fix missing replication
briefs.altText: Experimental-design diagram contrasting a two-room pseudoreplicated comparison with independent treatment units, subsamples, randomization, and blocking.
briefs.caption: Replication is determined by independent treatment assignment, not by the number of measurements taken inside one treatment unit.

briefs.exampleTitle: Higher light is correlated with higher yield
briefs.primaryMessage: A correlation between light and yield can reflect causation, reverse relationships, confounding, or selection effects.
layout: Confounder examples: cultivar, CO2, density, room, season
Conclusion language ladder: association → stronger causal support
forbiddenClaims: Do not imply correlation proves cause
Do not use statistical strength as proof of causation
Do not hide variables that changed with light
briefs.altText: Causal-reasoning diagram showing a light-yield correlation, alternative explanations, potential confounders, and stronger controlled designs.
briefs.caption: Correlation is useful evidence, but causal claims require designs that address timing and credible alternative explanations.
